decorous

/DEK-er-uhs/ - the stress falls on DEK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Decorous means socially proper and dignified.

Applause at the chess final was decorous — a soft patter of fingertips, never a whoop.

Example

At the embassy garden party, the interns were models of decorous conduct: they waited to be introduced, kept their voices beneath the string quartet, and declined the last éclair with a small apologetic bow.

Decorous is sharper than 'polite' because it measures conduct against what a social occasion calls for—not just kindness, but a bearing of dignity that fits the moment.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dignified: Dignified describes a person's own bearing — calm, serious, worthy of respect — wherever they happen to be. Decorous measures conduct against the occasion instead: decorous behavior is whatever this particular ceremony or gathering calls for. A judge is dignified by temperament; her courtroom manners are decorous.

seemly: Seemly is an older word for behavior that looks right and proper to onlookers — nothing about it would raise an eyebrow. Decorous asks for more than the absence of anything unfitting: decorous conduct actively carries the dignity a particular occasion calls for.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

rowdy: loud and rough where quiet dignity is expected

coarse: crude in manner, ignoring social polish

Where it sits · how much formality shapes the conduct — polite → decorous → ceremonious

polite vs. decorous: Polite stops short of decorous — politeness covers small courtesies, while decorous conduct is a whole bearing of dignity.

ceremonious vs. decorous: Ceremonious goes further than decorous — every bow and greeting follows a full script of formal ritual.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — decor-

Root — decor-: grace, what is fitting (Latin decor)

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: full of

Put it together

Put it together: Decor- (grace, what is fitting) + -ous (full of) = full of what is fitting. Latin decor named the grace of things done properly, and its noun decorum still means exactly that in English. Decorous behavior is behavior with the fittingness built in — measured, dignified, right for the room.

Use the root in a new word: decorum

Use the root in a new word: decorum: The umpire warned both dugouts to maintain decorum for the rest of the game.

Word Choice

formal

Decorous praises conduct that suits a dignified occasion — funerals, courtrooms, state dinners. For everyday niceness, 'polite' or 'well-behaved' is plainer. Its unit-mate punctilious goes narrower still: the punctilious person tracks every fine rule of form, while the decorous one simply carries the occasion's dignity.
